title: Hindsight Bias Through Knowledge Updating: A Conceptual Replication of Groß et al. (2023)

source.title: Hindsight Bias Through Knowledge Updating: A Conceptual Replication of Groß et al. (2023)
source.authors: Barbara K. Kreis, Antje Hermann, Thorsten Pachur, and Julia Groß

studies.title: Preregistered online experiment: hindsight bias and transfer learning for the sugar content of food items
studies.description: Single empirical study (N = 300 analysed) with a 3 (task: OJ, ROJ, NJ) by 4 (group: control, feedback, domain information, irrelevant information) mixed design. Appendices B (priors), C (mapping knowledge) and D (anchoring) are further analyses of the same sample, not separate experiments.

evidence.quote: In a high-powered conceptual replication (N = 300), we tested whether the findings generalize to the sugar content of food items—a domain where people are more familiar with both content and numerical range (up to 50 grams).
However, it is unclear whether hindsight bias and knowledge updating are equally influenced by familiarity and whether the degree of familiarity impacts the observed association between them.
From this knowledge-updating-and-rejudgment perspective, hindsight bias is a consequence of adaptive information integration, rather than reflecting a cognitive error.

Hindsight bias occurs when people estimate a quantity or predict an event’s outcome, learn the actual value or result, and then recall their initial judgment as being closer to the truth than it actually was.
this issue by conducting a preregistered (https://osf.io/2pr76) conceptual replication of Groß et al. (2023) for another domain, namely, the sugar content of food items.

First, presenting actual values for a set of objects should not only elicit hindsight bias for those objects, but also prompt an update of the underlying metric knowledge for the whole domain, leading to improved estimates for both the original objects and other objects from the domain (i.e., transfer learning).

Participants first completed an estimation task for a set of objects (original judgments, OJs). In an information phase, they were then presented with the actual values for those same objects (feedback group), the values for other objects in the same domain (domain-information group), or the actual values for the original objects but relabeled as belonging to another domain (irrelevant-information group). In the control group, no actual values were presented. Instead, participants read a text unrelated to the topic of the study.
Participants were then asked to recall their original estimates (recall of original judgments, ROJs) and to provide estimates for a new set of objects (new judgments, NJs).
If the ROJs are closer to the actual values than the OJs, then this would suggest the presence of hindsight effects
closer to the actual values than the OJs, then this would suggest the presence of transfer learning effects.

First, we expected that presenting the actual sugar content values for a set of previously estimated food items would both trigger hindsight effects for those food items and improve estimation accuracy for new food items (hindsight and transfer learning effects in the feedback group).

Second, we expected that not only presenting actual sugar content values for a set of previously estimated food items but also presenting values for other items from the same domain would also both trigger hindsight effects for the previously estimated items and improve estimation accuracy for new food items (hindsight and transfer learning effects in the domain-information group).

Third, we expected that presenting the actual sugar content values but relabeled as referring to an unrelated domain—here, longitudes of European cities—would not lead to either hindsight effects or improved estimation accuracy for new food items (no hindsight or transfer learning effects in the irrelevant-information group).

Finally, we did not expect to observe hindsight or transfer learning effects in the control group, where no actual values were presented (no hindsight or transfer learning effects in the control group).

The experiment was conducted online. Participants were recruited through Prolific (www.prolific.co) with the same general eligibility criteria as in the original study by Groß et al. (2023, Exp. 2): Participation was limited to native German speakers aged 18 to 45 years.

Additionally, we required that the study was conducted on a laptop, desktop computer, or tablet, rather than a smartphone. This was to ensure that the items, which were accompanied by food images, were properly displayed. We additionally excluded individuals who reported type 1 or type 2 diabetes or an eating disorder (e.g., anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder).
participants received a fixed compensation of £4.80.
Overall,N = 340 participants completed the experiment. They were, on average, 27.9 years old, with142 identifying as women,193 as men, and5 as diverse.

In the present study, most participants reported a university degree as their highest level of education (157), followed by a certificate of higher secondary education (122), vocational training (24), a certificate of lower secondary education (24), and a PhD (13).
The target sample size for the present study was determined by conducting an a priori frequentist simulation-based power analysis

As in the original study by Groß et al. (2023), we used 96 items. These were taken from eight food subcategories (grains and grain products; vegetables; fruit; milk and dairy products; fish, meat, and sausage; oils and fats; drinks; and sweets and snacks), with each subcategory containing 12 items

we included an image and specified the weight of each food item (e.g., “How many grams of sugar are in a kiwi that weighs 85 grams?”) to clarify the size of the food item and increase ecological validity

For most items, participants were asked to estimate the sugar content of a typical serving size, such as a banana; for others, the sugar content of a typical purchase size, such as a can of coconut milk.
The food items varied in sugar content (M = 7.6 grams, SD = 7.7, min = 0, max = 33)
We photographed all items and edited the pictures to blur any visible labels, nutritional information, and numbers.
All food images are available at https://osf.io/hr5bv/.

From these 96 items, we created three sets of 32 items each. Each set contained four items from each of the eight food subcategories (see Appendix A2 for details). The sets were designed to be comparable in terms of degree of processing and statistical characteristics of the sugar content (mean, median, range).

In the experiment, one set of items was presented to all groups in both the OJ and ROJ task. In the information phase, actual values for the same set were presented to participants in the feedback group; the same values, but relabeled as longitudes of European cities (which have a similar numerical range to the sugar content values), to participants in the irrelevant-information group. Participants in the domain-information group were presented with values for a second set of food items. Finally, all groups were presented with a third set of food times in the NJ task.

It consisted of four phases: Participants (1) completed the OJ task, (2) were presented with actual values of different types depending on the experimental group to which they were randomly assigned, (3) completed the ROJ task, and (4) completed the NJ task. This resulted in a three (task: OJ, ROJ, NJ) by four (group: control, feedback, domain information, irrelevant information) mixed design.

After providing informed consent, participants entered the first phase, the OJ task, where they estimated the sugar content of 32 food items (e.g., “How many grams of sugar does a kiwi that weighs 85 grams contain?”). The items were presented sequentially in a randomized order for each participant.

This domain was selected to match the mean and range of the sugar content values across the three sets (see Appendix A2 for details).

In the fourth and final phase, the NJ task, participants estimated the sugar content of a new set of 32 food items (“How many grams of sugar does a tangerine that weighs 90 grams contain?”). The assignment of sets was counterbalanced, with each set being presented with comparable frequency across participants and experimental groups.

After completing all four phases, participants were asked whether they had cheated or clicked through the experiment and whether they had any problems with the display of images, before indicating their prior engagement with the domain. Finally, they had the opportunity to enter any additional comments into an open response field.

First, Prolific automatically excluded participants who did not finish the experiment within the specified 87-minute time limit. Second, we excluded all participants whose meta-data indicated that contrary to the eligibility criteria they had used a smartphone (six participants). Third, we excluded participants who indicated non-compliance, such as cheating (one participant) or just clicking through the experiment (one participant). Fourth, we excluded participants who reported technical problems or disruptions (two participants who reloaded the experiment, one participant who reported a disturbance that led to a long break during the experiment, and three participants who reported problems with the display of several food images). Fifth, we excluded one participant for providing estimates that exceeded the weight of the food item for 10 or more items, as such sugar content is not possible. Sixth, we planned to exclude cases in which participants provided estimates in under 1000 ms for 10 or more items, as such short estimation processes are implausible; however, there were no such cases.
Seventh, we excluded 21 participants whose estimates had a median absolute deviation from the actual values (see Eq. 1 below)

Overall, the results of the present study replicate those of the original study (Groß et al., 2023, Exp. 2), with few exceptions. Unless noted otherwise, the observed patterns of results are identical.

To test for transfer learning effects, we compared a model including the fixed-effect predictor task (OJ versus NJ) to a baseline model that did not include the predictor.

As expected, in both experimental groups that saw domain-relevant values, there were transfer learning effects (feedback group: b =−6.59, CI 95% = [−8.63,−4.55], BF10 > 10, 000; domain-information group: b =−3.71, CI 95% = [−5.09,−2.32], BF10 > 10, 000).
An interaction analysis indicated that the transfer learning effect was larger in the feedback group than in the domain-information group (b =−3.11,CI 95% = [−5.06,−1.16], BF10 = 11).

There was no transfer learning effect in the irrelevant-information group (b = 0.52, CI 95% = [−0.45, 1.49], BF10 = 0.08) or the control group (b =−0.92, CI 95% = [−2.00, 0.15], BF10 = 0.19), with an interaction analysis indicating no difference between these two groups (b = 1.35, CI 95% = [−0.06, 2.77], BF10 = 0.37).
In contrast, in Groß et al. (2023, Exp. 2), the size of the effect did not differ between the two groups.
To test for hindsight effects, we compared a model including the fixed-effect predictor task (OJ versus ROJ) to a baseline model that did not include the predictor.

As expected, there was a hindsight effect in the feedback group (b =−2.88, CI 95% = [−4.19,−1.54], BF10 = 268). Importantly, there was also a hindsight effect in the domain-information group (b =−2.25, CI 95% = [−3.32,−1.16], BF10 = 80). An interaction analysis showed that the size of the hindsight effect did not differ between these two groups (b =−0.70, CI 95% = [−2.11, 0.71], BF10 = 0.07).

Critically, there was no hindsight effect in the irrelevant-information group (b = 0.87, CI 95% = [−0.06, 1.81], BF10 = 0.23) or the control group (b = 1.10, CI 95% = [−0.15, 2.35], BF10 = 0.25), with an interaction analysis indicating no difference between the control and the irrelevant-information
However, additional analyses showed no indication for such alternative influences of the relabeled values (for details, see Appendix D, and Groß et al., 2023).

In sum, the results replicate the key novel finding of Groß et al. (2023, Exp. 2). Hindsight effects were triggered for objects even when participants were presented with the values of other objects in the same domain, not only when they were presented with the actual values of the original objects.

First, the initial accuracy of the ranking of objects, quantified as the rank-order correlation between estimates and actual values in the OJ task, was higher for sugar content (ρ = 0.61) than for country populations (ρ = 0.52; Groß et al., 2023)

Food subcategories with higher initial estimation accuracy showed smaller transfer learning and hindsight effects, while those with lower initial estimation accuracy showed greater transfer learning and hindsight effects.
for the Oils and fats subcategory, where initial estimation accuracy was rather high
In both the feedback and the domain-information groups, hindsight effects were smaller than transfer learning effects, with the ROJs being further away from the actual values than the NJs
However, the results of the present study indicate that processes other than knowledge updating might also contribute to hindsight bias.
Thus, participants seem to engage in additional processes in the ROJ task (e.g., adjusting the ROJ using episodic memory traces of the OJ to account for inaccuracies in initial estimation).
It is conceivable, however, that the contribution of anchoring-and-adjustment processes depends on the order of presentation of actual values and ROJ task.

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Preregistered online between-groups experiment with a within-person task factor (conceptual replication of Groß et al., 2023, Exp. 2)

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Participants estimate the sugar content of 32 food items (original judgments, OJ), then see numerical information that differs by group (actual values for the same items, values for other food items, the same values relabeled as longitudes of European cities, or an unrelated text), then recall their original estimates (ROJ) and estimate 32 new food items (NJ). Hindsight effects (ROJ closer to the actual values than OJ) and transfer learning effects (NJ closer than OJ) are compared across groups.

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Does the link between hindsight bias and knowledge updating found by Groß et al. (2023) for country populations generalize to a domain people know better, the sugar content of food items?

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: It is unclear whether hindsight bias and knowledge updating are equally influenced by familiarity and whether familiarity changes the association between them; the original domain (country populations, numbers in the millions) is unfamiliar.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: Knowledge-updating account: hindsight bias is a by-product of adaptive updating of the knowledge base; recalling an initial judgment then means re-judging the object with updated knowledge. The traditional view is anchoring and adjustment (cognitive error).

fields.label: Key concepts
fields.value: Hindsight effect: |Δ| smaller for ROJs than OJs. Transfer learning effect: |Δ| smaller for NJs than OJs. Seed facts: actual values presented for a set of objects. Three derived predictions: transfer learning for the whole domain, hindsight via domain information, no hindsight via irrelevant information.

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: The replication reproduces the key results of Groß et al. (2023, Exp. 2): hindsight effects occur with feedback and with domain information, and not with relabeled irrelevant information or without values.

fields.label: Support
fields.value: Hindsight and transfer learning effects co-occurred in the feedback and domain-information groups (Bayes factors in the results); with few exceptions (larger transfer effect in feedback than in domain group; mapping knowledge also improved).

fields.label: Mechanism proposed
fields.value: Knowledge updating and rejudgment; additional processes (such as adjusting ROJs with episodic memory traces of the OJ) may contribute because hindsight effects were smaller than transfer learning effects.

fields.label: Contribution
fields.value: Shows the link between hindsight bias and knowledge updating generalizes to a more familiar domain and numerical range.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: One domain (sugar content of food items), German-speaking Prolific participants aged 18 to 45, online; the domain is argued to be more familiar than country populations.

fields.label: Stated limitations and open issues
fields.value: All actual values were presented before any ROJ; anchoring might play a larger role if values and ROJs alternated. Mean-centering the criterion and excluding perfect OJ/ROJ pairs for transfer learning were not preregistered.

fields.label: Replication
fields.value: This study is a conceptual replication of Groß et al. (2023, Exp. 2); deviations in measure (|Δ| instead of order-of-magnitude error), materials (images, weight), presentation time (8 s versus 5 s) and exclusions.

fields.label: Openness
fields.value: Preregistration at https://osf.io/2pr76; data, code, materials and images at https://osf.io/hr5bv/ (URLs recorded, not consulted).

fields.label: Steps
fields.value: Phases OJ, information, ROJ and NJ and the post-experiment engagement question can be replayed as text. Consent, device checks, Prolific time limits, display problems and response-time exclusions cannot be replayed.

fields.label: Roles
fields.value: Every participant is an AI participant, run sequentially with its own conversation history. No scripted roles exist in the paper.

fields.label: Conditions
fields.value: Feedback, domain-information and irrelevant-information arms can run from printed materials (city–value pairing and countries are assumptions to confirm). The control arm cannot run until the filler text is supplied.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: |Δ| per task, hindsight and transfer effects per group; the paper's Bayesian mixed models are not reproduced offline (approximate paired comparisons only). Prior engagement is a self-report of real-world experience and is not simulated.

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: AI participants have no real food experience, time pressure, reaction times or visual perception of the images (text only unless images are supplied); an AI that keeps its transcript can reproduce its OJ exactly in the ROJ task, which differs from human memory.

issues.title: Instruction and consent texts are not printed
issues.reason: Only example question wordings are printed; instruction screens, response-field label and consent text are not.
issues.impact: The replay needs minimal framing around the printed questions; wording could influence estimates.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the original (German) instruction screens or approve a minimal framing.

issues.title: Food images are not available
issues.reason: The images are on OSF (not consulted) and are not in the paper.
issues.impact: AI participants see text only; images were part of the stimulus and clarified item size.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the images or accept a text-only replay.

issues.title: Filler text for the control group is missing
issues.reason: The text is described as unrelated to the study but not printed.
issues.impact: The control arm cannot run without inventing text, and the paper's control comparisons need it.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the filler text in materials/materials.json (control_filler_text).

issues.title: City–value pairing, countries and flags are not printed
issues.reason: Only the Basel example and the city list with approximate longitudes are given.
issues.impact: Pairing by rank (supported by the Basel–kiwi example) and omitting countries and flags are assumptions.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm the pairing and supply country names or flags.

issues.title: Counterbalancing scheme for item sets is not described
issues.impact: The replay uses a rotation over the six assignments of sets to roles; real scheme may differ.

issues.title: Group allocation procedure and randomized n are not reported
issues.reason: Random assignment is stated; allocation ratio and the numbers randomized per group are not.
issues.impact: The replay allocates equal n per arm.

issues.title: Order of values in the information phase is not stated
issues.reason: The step description gives timing (8 s per item) but not the order.
issues.impact: The replay shows values in a random order per participant.

issues.title: Two printed OJ wordings differ
issues.reason: Figure 1 text reads 'How many grams of sugar are in a kiwi that weighs 85 grams?' and the procedure example reads 'How many grams of sugar does a kiwi that weighs 85 grams contain?'; both are translations.
issues.impact: Item wording in the replay follows the procedure example.

issues.title: MCMC settings, coding and outlier reference are not stated
issues.reason: Chains, iterations, task coding and the exact threefold-IQR rule are not given.
issues.impact: Bayes factors cannot be reproduced offline; evaluate() reports approximate paired comparisons and marks Bayes factors not_ready.

issues.title: Outlier criterion not fully specified
issues.reason: Seventh exclusion step lacks the reference for the interquartile range.
issues.impact: evaluate() uses Q3 + 3 × IQR of person-level median absolute deviations per task.

issues.title: Cell means of |Δ| are not reported numerically
issues.impact: The simulation cannot be compared with exact human means.
issues.suggestedAction: Obtain means from the OSF data.

issues.title: Wording of compliance and display questions is not printed
issues.impact: Not replayable; AI participants are not asked.

issues.title: Units and phrasing for liquid and counted items are not printed
issues.reason: Table A1 gives size in g or ml without marking which; examples only cover solid items with 'weighs … grams'.
issues.impact: The replay uses the printed pattern with the sizes as grams, including for drinks.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm the original item phrasing and units.

issues.title: Allocation procedure for random assignment is not stated
issues.reason: The paper says participants were randomly assigned but not how.
issues.impact: The replay allocates equal n per arm.
